claim: Model-based reasoning relies on a circuit that includes the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: Using knowledge of the structure of the world to infer value is at the heart of model-based reasoning, and relies on a circuit that includes the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) (Stalnaker et al., 2015; Rudebeck and Murray, 2014; Wallis, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Stalnaker et al., 2015; Rudebeck and Murray, 2014; Wallis, 2011).

claim: When OFC is intact, rats and primates can use the causal structure of their environment to infer the value of elements on-the-fly.
source: When OFC is intact, rats and primates can use the causal structure of their environment to infer the value of elements on-the-fly.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating this effect in various situations.

claim: With OFC inactivated or lesioned, rats and primates cannot use the causal structure of their environment to infer value.
source: With OFC inactivated or lesioned, they cannot.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies showing this effect (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Reber et al., 2017; Gremel and Costa, 2013; West et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2009; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010).

claim: Inactivation of the OFC entirely and selectively impairs the use of previously acquired stimulus-stimulus associations to guide responding during sensory preconditioning.
source: Here, inactivation of the OFC entirely and selectively impairs the use of previously acquired stimulus-stimulus associations to guide responding when one of the cues later comes to predict food (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2012.

claim: Some proposals focus on the ability of OFC neurons to respond to cues based on their acquired biological significance or value.
source: Some proposals focus on the ability of OFC neurons to respond to cues based on their acquired biological significance or value (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Rolls, 1996; Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Rolls et al., 1996; Rolls and Grabenhorst, 2008; Kringelbach, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies proposing this view.

claim: Inactivation or lesions of OFC typically only affect value-guided behavior that requires inference or model-based processing.
source: However, inactivation or lesions of OFC typically only affect value-guided behavior that requires inference or model-based processing (Schoenbaum et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schoenbaum et al., 2011.

claim: If the value can be derived from direct experience, the OFC is not normally necessary.
source: If the value can be derived from direct experience, the OFC is not normally necessary.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of OFC involvement in different types of tasks.

claim: The OFC may be required for representing the model rather than uniquely for encoding value.
source: This raises the possibility that the OFC is required for representing the model and perhaps not, uniquely, for encoding value (Wilson et al., 2014; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2014 and Schuck et al., 2016.

claim: If the core function of the OFC is to represent associative information that has biological significance or value, then this area should not represent neutral associations until they have acquired some significance.
source: If the core function of the OFC is to represent associative information that has biological significance or value, then this area should not represent such neutral associations until they have acquired some significance.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from one theoretical account of OFC function.

claim: If the core function of the OFC is to represent the causal structure of the world, then one might expect to see neutral relationships represented in some manner, even before they have any significance.
source: On the other hand, if the core function of the OFC is to represent the causal structure of the world, then one might expect to see these relationships represented in some manner, even before they have any significance.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from an alternative theoretical account of OFC function.

claim: 21 rats with recording electrodes implanted in the OFC were trained in a sensory-preconditioning task.
source: We trained 21 rats with recording electrodes implanted in the OFC in a sensory-preconditioning task similar to the one used in our prior study (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the initial phase, rats learned to associate two pairs of 10 s auditory cues (A->B; C->D) in the absence of reward.
source: In the initial phase, rats learned to associate two pairs of 10 s auditory cues (A->B; C->D) in the absence of reward.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: During preconditioning, rats showed no significant responding at the food cup and no differences among the different cues.
source: As there was no reward, rats showed no significant responding at the food cup and no differences among the different cues (one-way ANOVA, F(3, 80)=0.54, p=0.66; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and Figure 1A showing behavioral data.

claim: In the second phase, rats learned that one of the auditory cues (B) predicted reward and the other (D) did not.
source: In the second phase, rats learned that one of the auditory cues (B) predicted reward and the other (D) did not.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: Learning during conditioning was reflected in an increase in responding at the food cup during presentation of B, but not D.
source: Learning during conditioning was reflected in an increase in responding at the food cup during presentation of B, but not D (two-way ANOVA, main effect of cue: F(1, 246)=46.95, p<0.001, main effect of session: F(5, 246)=11.75, p<0.001 interaction: F(5, 246)=3.49 p=0.0046; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) and Figure 1B showing behavioral data.

claim: In the final phase, rats responded at the food cup significantly more to cue B than D.
source: As expected, the rats responded at the food cup significantly more to cue B than D (Figure 1C, left panel; t-testBD: t(20) = 8.23)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and Figure 1C showing behavioral data.

claim: Rats responded more during presentation of A, the cue that predicted B, than during presentation of C, the cue that predicted D.
source: more during presentation of A, the cue that predicted B, than during presentation of C, the cue that predicted D (Figure 1C, central panel; ANOVA, main effect of cue: F(1, 251)=5.79, df = 1, p=0.017; t-testAC: t(20) = 2.15, df = 1, p=0.044).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA and t-test) and Figure 1C showing behavioral data.

claim: 266 neurons were recorded from OFC during the two preconditioning days.
source: We recorded 266 neurons from OFC during the two preconditioning days (an average of 6 neurons per subject per day).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data collected.

claim: 42% of OFC neurons significantly increased firing to at least one of the cues during preconditioning.
source: Of these, 42% (112/266) significantly increased firing to at least one of the cues during preconditioning (right-tailed rank-sum between baseline and cue response, p<0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (rank-sum test) of neural data.

claim: 15% of OFC neurons significantly decreased firing during preconditioning.
source: while 15% significantly decreased firing (40/266; left-tailed rank-sum, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (rank-sum test) of neural data.

claim: The prevalence of modulated firing to each of the individual cues was roughly equivalent during preconditioning.
source: Overall, the prevalence of modulated firing to each of the individual cues was roughly equivalent (excited: 20% A, 18% B, 20% C, 13% D; inhibited: 7% A, 7% B, 4% C, 2% D).
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptive statistics of neural responses.

claim: Elevated firing to both cues of a pair (A and B or C and D) was more common than elevated firing to cues of different pairs (A and D or B and C).
source: This population included some neurons responding to one or both cue pairs, and such correlates were over-represented in the population of neurons responding to at least one of the cues, with elevated firing to both cues of a pair (A and B or C and D, 45/112) more common than elevated firing to cues of different pairs (A and D or B and C, 23/112; chi-squared test for independence, X2 = 10.2; p=0.0014).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of neural data.

claim: Neurons that respond to one cue of a pair have a strong tendency to respond to the other cue of that pair.
source: This plot shows that those neurons that respond to one cue of a pair (e.g., cue A) have a strong tendency to respond to the other cue of a pair (e.g. B), confirming the pattern seen in individual neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2A and 2B showing neural response patterns.

claim: OFC neurons were much more likely to have a similar response to paired cues (AB or CD) than to unpaired cues (CB, AD).
source: As illustrated in Figure 2C, we found that OFC neurons were much more likely to have a similar response to paired cues (AB or CD) than to unpaired cues (CB, AD). This was true across all neurons (n = 266 rhoAB=0.74 and rhoCB = 0.16, Zr1-r2 = 9.05, p<10−16; rhoCD = 0.75, rhoAD = 0.23, Zr1-r2 = 8.59, p<10−16).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (correlation and Fisher r-to-z transformation) and Figure 2C showing correlation data.

claim: OFC neurons tended to respond similarly to the paired auditory cues and distinctly to each of the pairs.
source: Thus, OFC neurons tended to respond similarly to the paired auditory cues and distinctly to each of the pairs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the correlation analyses presented.

claim: Temporal contiguity of the time bins does not account for the correlated firing observed in OFC during the cues in preconditioning.
source: These results suggest that mere temporal contiguity of the time bins does not account for the correlated firing observed in OFC during the cues in preconditioning.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 comparing correlations at different temporal distances.

claim: On day 1 of preconditioning, the correlations were strongest on the same trial for each cue of a pair, weaker for adjacent trials of that pair, and negligible between the early trials of one cue of the pair and the late trials of the other cue of the pair.
source: on day 1, the correlations were strongest on the same trial for each cue of a pair, weaker for adjacent trials of that pair, and negligible between the early trials of one cue of the pair and the late trials of the other cue of the pair.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: On day 2 of preconditioning, the correlations between cues of a pair encompass most of the 6 trials of the opposite pair of each cue, forming more of a checkerboard pattern.
source: However on day 2, following a full day of preconditioning and time to consolidate associations, the correlations between cues of a pair encompass most of the 6 trials of the opposite pair of each cue, forming more of a checkerboard pattern, as if a reliable response is evoked to each cue of a pair.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The across-trial reliability of the evoked response is consistent with identification of the cue pairs as a reliable feature of the environment in these rats.
source: The across-trial reliability of the evoked response is consistent with identification of the cue pairs as a reliable feature of the environment in these rats.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data pattern observed in Figure 3A.

claim: On day two of preconditioning, the ability to classify B and D is nearly perfect at telling their paired partners (A and C) apart.
source: On day one the ability to classify trials as B (black grid background) or D (grey grid background) does not discriminate the paired cues (A and C) very well, whereas the ability to classify B and D on day two is nearly perfect at telling their paired partners apart.
evidence: The claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The population response showed a decline in self-classification and an increase in within-pair classification across the two preconditioning days.
source: When the output of these classifiers are aggregated by response (correct, or within and between pair errors), displayed in Figure 3D, the population response showed a decline in self-classification and an increase in within-pair classification across the two preconditioning days.
evidence: The claim is supported by the classification analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The shift in within-pair classification across days was unlikely to occur by chance (p=0.009).
source: According to this approach, which allows the direct calculation of a p-value for the specific difference that was observed, the shift in within-pair classification across days was unlikely to occur by chance (p=0.009, Figure 3E, top panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by permutation test analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The difference between the within pair and between pair classification on day two was unlikely to occur by chance (p=0.0001).
source: A similar permutation test on the difference between the within pair and between pair classification on day two found that this difference was also unlikely to occur by chance (p=0.0001, Figure 3D, top right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by permutation test analysis.

claim: After controlling for baseline differences, there was an increase in within-pair classification from day 1 to day 2 (psubtraction = 0.001; presidual = 0.007).
source: In both, we again observed an increase in within-pair classification from day 1 to day 2 (psubtraction = 0.001; presidual = 0.007)
evidence: The claim is supported by control analyses using baseline-corrected data.

claim: After controlling for baseline differences, there was a greater within-pair than between pair classification on day 2 (psubtraction = 0.011; presidual = 0.038).
source: and a greater within-pair than between pair classification on day 2 (psubtraction = 0.011; presidual = 0.038).
evidence: The claim is supported by control analyses using baseline-corrected data.

claim: Activity to B increased significantly in the 683 neurons recorded over the course of 6 days of conditioning.
source: Accordingly, we found that activity to B increased significantly in the 683 neurons recorded over the course of 6 days of conditioning.
evidence: The claim is supported by neural data collected during conditioning.

claim: Over the 6 days of training, cue B comes to evoke a larger neural response than cue D.
source: Firing to cues B and D is initially very similar, however over the 6 days of training, cue B comes to evoke a larger neural response than cue D.
evidence: The claim is supported by neural data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: On the final conditioning day, twice as many neurons fired above baseline in the first 2 s of cue B than did so at the outset of cue D.
source: On the final conditioning day, twice as many neurons fired above baseline in the first 2 s of cue B, before reward onset, than did so at the outset of cue D (17%, 17/101 vs 7%, 7/101; X2 = 4.73, p=0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of neural data.

claim: The prevalence of neurons responding to cue B increased significantly over the course of conditioning.
source: In addition, the prevalence of such neurons increased significantly over the course of conditioning for rewarded cue B (17% or 17/101 on day 6 vs 8% or 10/128 on day 1; X2 = 4.41, p=0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of neural data.

claim: The prevalence of neurons responding to cue D did not increase significantly over the course of conditioning.
source: vs cue D (7% or 7/101 on day 6 vs 6% or 8/128 on day 1; X2 = 0.04, p=0.84).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-squared test) of neural data.

claim: 205 neurons were recorded in the probe session.
source: To examine this, we plotted the activity of the 205 neurons (averaging 9.8 neurons per subject) recorded in the probe session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data collected.

claim: A larger fraction of neurons exhibited increased activity to the rewarded cue B than cue D in the probe test (31% vs 8%).
source: Consistent with the conditioning data, a larger fraction of neurons again exhibited increased activity to the rewarded cue B than cue D (31% vs 8%; one-way sign-test baseline vs. cue, Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (sign-test) and Figure 5A showing neural data.

claim: The fraction of neurons responding above baseline to the preconditioned cues (A and C) increased significantly in the probe test.
source: However, in addition, the fraction of neurons responding above baseline to the preconditioned cues (A and C) also increased significantly (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5A showing neural data.

claim: 37% of neurons elevated their firing rate to cue A in the probe test.
source: Notably, although the firing to each remained largely segregated, the increase was seen to both cues, with 37% of neurons elevating their firing rate to cue A
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (sign-test) of neural data.

claim: 35% of neurons elevated their firing rate to cue C in the probe test.
source: and 35% of neurons elevating their firing rate to cue C (across first 3 trials of each for comparison with B/D fractions, one-way sign-test, baseline vs. cue, p<0.05)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (sign-test) of neural data.

claim: In neurons with the stronger response to A, there is a strong and prolonged response to cue B (and reward).
source: In neurons with the stronger response to A, there is a strong and prolonged response to cue B (and reward)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In neurons with the stronger response to C, there was only a modest response to cue B, primarily observed only after reward delivery begins.
source: whereas in neurons with the stronger response to C, there was only a modest response to cue B, and this response is primarily observed only after reward delivery begins.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The activity of OFC neurons integrates associations formed in preconditioning and conditioning in the probe test.
source: The increase in the fraction of neurons responding to cues A and C, which had not been presented since preconditioning, coupled with the preserved relationship between firing to cues A and B, shows that the activity of OFC neurons integrates associations formed in preconditioning and conditioning in the probe test.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the neural data patterns observed.

claim: Conditioned responding to cue A in the probe test is OFC-dependent.
source: As noted earlier, conditioned responding in this phase to cue A is OFC-dependent (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2012.

claim: For neurons recorded in rats that responded more to cue A than to cue C, there was stronger correlated firing between formerly paired cues than between cues that had never been paired.
source: These neurons showed stronger correlated firing between formerly paired cues than between cues that had never been paired (n = 150, rhoAB = 0.43 and rhoCB = 0.19, Zr1-r2= 2.27, p=0.023; rhoCD = 0.37, rhoAD = 0.12, Zr1-r2 = 2.36, p=0.018).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (correlation and Fisher r-to-z transformation) shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For neurons recorded in rats that showed either no preference in responding to cues A and C or responded more to cue C than cue A, correlated firing between the unpaired cues was as strong or stronger than that between the formerly paired cues.
source: These neurons showed correlated firing between the unpaired cues that was as strong or stronger than that between the formerly paired cues (n = 55, rhoAB = 0.45 and rhoCB = 0.59, Zr1-r2 = 0.90, p=0.36; rhoCD = 0.12, rhoAD = 0.14, Zr1-r2 = 0.13, p=0.89).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (correlation and Fisher r-to-z transformation) shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Classification accuracy for the ensemble recorded in rats that exhibited evidence of preconditioning was significantly above chance for the majority of bins during the second half of cue B.
source: By this measure, classification accuracy for the ensemble recorded in rats that exhibited evidence of preconditioning was significantly above chance for the majority of bins during the second half of cue B, when cue B was co-presented with rewarding food pellets.
evidence: The claim is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Classification accuracy for the ensemble recorded in rats that did not appear to precondition hovered near chance for all bins.
source: By contrast classification accuracy for the ensemble recorded in rats that did not appear to precondition hovered near chance for all bins.
evidence: The claim is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Above-chance classification was only observed in ensembles composed of neurons from good performers.
source: The result, plotted separately for the neurons recorded in good (Figure 6C) and poor (Figure 6D) performers, shows that above-chance classification (e.g. B = A and D = C) was only observed in ensembles composed of neurons from good performers.
evidence: The claim is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The significant increase in correct classification came during the period when cue B overlapped with reward and was consistent through this period.
source: Further, the significant increase in correct classification came during the period when cue B overlapped with reward and was consistent through this period.
evidence: The claim is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Activity during A is directly signaling B and its association with reward, even though A was never presented with reward.
source: This indicates not only that the ensembles reorganized in the good performers as a result of conditioning, but that they reorganized such that activity during A was best correlated with the middle and later sections of B, when reward could be expected to come. This is consistent with the idea that activity during A is directly signaling B and is association with reward, even though A was never presented with reward.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification analysis results.

claim: OFC acquires neural representations of the arbitrary cue pairs in the initial phase of preconditioning, prior to the introduction of reward.
source: That OFC acquires neural representations of the arbitrary cue pairs in the initial phase of preconditioning, prior to the introduction of reward, suggests that the OFC builds associative representations even for information that does not have clear biological significance or value.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the preconditioning neural data.

claim: The OFC builds associative representations even for information that does not have clear biological significance or value.
source: That OFC acquires neural representations of the arbitrary cue pairs in the initial phase of preconditioning, prior to the introduction of reward, suggests that the OFC builds associative representations even for information that does not have clear biological significance or value.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Implicit learning of statistical relationships between visual or auditory cues has been reported in sensory cortices.
source: While the implicit learning of statistical relationships between visual (Turk-Browne et al., 2009) or auditory cues (McNealy et al., 2006) has been reported in sensory cortices
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Turk-Browne et al., 2009 and McNealy et al., 2006.

claim: It is striking that more frontal regions like OFC have access to statistical associations between cues.
source: it's striking that more frontal regions like OFC have access to these associations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior literature.

claim: Hippocampal, retrosplenial, striatal, and even midbrain areas appear to be involved in and even required for stimulus-stimulus learning.
source: In this regard, the OFC joins a growing number of associative regions, including hippocampal, retrosplenial, striatal, and even midbrain areas (Cerri et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2014; Sharpe et al., 2017a; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012), that appear to be involved in and even required for stimulus-stimulus learning.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Cerri et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2014; Sharpe et al., 2017a; Wimmer and Shohamy, 2012).

claim: Successor representations capture the expectation of moving to one state from another, independent of value, but stop short of encoding a full task model.
source: These representations capture the expectation of moving to one state from another, independent of value, but stop short of encoding a full task model (Gershman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gershman et al., 2012.

claim: Successor representations have been applied to interpret neural activity in hippocampus.
source: Successor representations have been applied to interpret neural activity in hippocampus (Stachenfeld et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stachenfeld et al., 2017.

claim: In simple versions of successor representation models, an established matrix is not affected except by direct experience.
source: In simple versions of this model, an established matrix is not affected except by direct experience
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of successor representation models.

claim: A preconditioned cue will not serve as a conditioned reinforcer, whereas a second-order cue will do so.
source: Further, recent evidence shows that cue A in our design will not serve as a conditioned reinforcer, whereas a second-order cue will do so (Sharpe et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sharpe et al., 2017b.

claim: A preconditioned cue is not accessing cached value by any common definition.
source: These data provide direct evidence that a preconditioned cue, at least in our design, is not accessing cached value by any common definition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Sharpe et al., 2017b.

claim: The activity observed in OFC seems more consistent with the proposal that the OFC encodes a fuller cognitive 'state' map.
source: While these disparate findings can perhaps be reconciled with successor representations models that incorporate off-line rehearsal or other additional processing steps, the activity we observe here seems more consistent with the proposal that the OFC encodes a fuller cognitive 'state' map (Stalnaker et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2014; Lopatina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: The current results are consistent with data showing that the OFC is necessary for performance in the final phase of training in this task.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that the current results are consistent with data showing that the OFC is necessary for performance in the final phase of training in this task, when information must be integrated to predict the reward.
evidence: This is a statement connecting the current findings to prior work.

claim: Neural activity in the probe test to the preconditioned cues clearly differed between pairs.
source: Neural activity in the probe test to the preconditioned cues clearly differed between pairs
evidence: This is a summary of the neural data from the probe test.

claim: Activity in the first cue of a pair appeared to encode the second cue, particularly for the critical AC cue pair.
source: and activity in the first cue of a pair appeared to encode the second cue, particularly for the critical AC cue pair.
evidence: This is a summary of the neural data from the probe test.

claim: Activity to A was most similar to activity during the rewarded portions of B.
source: Activity to A was most similar to activity during the rewarded portions of B
evidence: This is a summary of the neural data from the probe test.

claim: The coding of A as similar to rewarded B was strongest in the rats that showed strong responding to A.
source: and this coding was strongest in the rats that showed strong responding to A.
evidence: This is a summary of the neural data from the probe test.

claim: The correlates in OFC may be merely a reflection of processing in other brain regions, such as the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex.
source: The correlates in OFC may be merely a reflection of processing in other brain regions, such as the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex, which are necessary in these earlier phases (Robinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the possible role of OFC, with a citation to Robinson et al., 2014.

claim: The OFC receives strong input from hippocampus, which has a specific influence on the encoding in OFC in real time.
source: Consistent with this idea, the OFC receives strong input from hippocampus, which has a specific influence on the encoding in OFC in real time (Wikenheiser et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wikenheiser et al., 2017.

claim: If OFC correlates are merely a reflection of processing in other brain regions, temporary inactivation of OFC during the preconditioning phase should not affect inference in the final test.
source: In this case, temporary inactivation of OFC during the preconditioning phase should not affect inference in the final test.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on one interpretation of the findings.

claim: If representation of sensory-sensory information in OFC is necessary in the preconditioning phase, then inactivation should affect later responding.
source: By contrast, representation of this information in OFC may be necessary in the preconditioning phase, perhaps to allow proper updating or integration with the new learning. If this is the case, then inactivation should affect later responding.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on an alternative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The identification of sensory-sensory representations in the OFC prior to their endowment with biological significance substantially expands the potential role of this area.
source: Regardless, the identification of sensory-sensory representations in the OFC prior to their endowment with biological significance substantially expands the potential role of this area in this very simple and other more complex settings.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Twenty-one adult male Long-Evans rats were used in the study.
source: Twenty-one adult male Long-Evans rats (weighing 275–325 g on arrival) were individually housed and given ad libitum access to food and water, except during behavioral training and testing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental subjects.

claim: During training and testing, rats were restricted to 10 g of standard rat chow, which they received following each training session.
source: During training and testing, they were restricted to 10 g of standard rat chow, which they received following each training session.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: Rats were maintained on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and trained and tested during the light cycle.
source: Rats were maintained on a 12 hr light/dark cycle and trained and tested during the light cycle.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: Experiments were performed at the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program, in accordance with NIH guidelines.
source: Experiments were performed at the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program, in accordance with NIH guidelines.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental location and ethical compliance.

claim: The number of subjects was chosen based on expectations of what was needed to detect behavioral and neural evidence of learning on each experimental day.
source: The number of subjects was chosen based on our expectations of what was needed to detect behavioral and neural evidence of learning on each experimental day (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design rationale, with a citation.

claim: Multi-electrode bundles (16 nichrome microwires attached to a microdrive) were inserted 0.5 mm above orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Multi-electrode bundles (16 nichrome microwires attached to a microdrive) were inserted 0.5 above orbitofrontal cortex [AP 3.2 mm and ML 3.0 mm relative to bregma (Paxinos and Watson, 2009); and DV 4.0 mm from the dura]
evidence: This is a direct statement of the surgical procedure.

claim: Electrodes were implanted unilaterally in 18 rats and bilaterally in two rats.
source: unilaterally in 18 rats and bilaterally in two rats.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the surgical procedure.

claim: For 18 rats, behavioral training began 2–3 weeks following electrode implantation.
source: For 18 rats, behavioral training began 2–3 weeks following electrode implantation
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental timeline.

claim: Three subjects began training 10–14 weeks following electrode implantation, after participation in an olfactory operant task with liquid rewards.
source: an additional three subjects began training 10–14 weeks following electrode implantation, after participation in an olfactory operant task with liquid rewards.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental timeline for a subset of subjects.

claim: In each day of preconditioning, rats received trials in which two pairs of auditory cues (A→B and C→D) were presented in a blocked design.
source: In each day of preconditioning, rats received trials in which two pairs of auditory cues (A→B and C→D) were presented in a blocked design.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental procedure.

claim: Each cue pair was presented six times during preconditioning.
